item.title: Nginx Reverse Proxy Design and Port Binding in a Next.js / NestJS Multi-Container Architecture
item.description:
Co-locating frontend and backend roles on a single application server and individually exposing public ports introduces bottlenecks in scaling out components and maintaining security. Particularly in microservice architectures and decoupled frontend/backend architectures, centralizing endpoints and isolating internal networks are essential. This document outlines the design and verification procedures for a multi-tier container architecture that decouples the frontend (Next.js), backend (NestJS), and database (MySQL), integrating Nginx as a unified entry point for ingress traffic.

Network Configuration and Container Topology

In this configuration, all external requests are received by the Nginx reverse proxy (Port 80) and routed to the appropriate service on the internal Docker bridge network based on the URI path. Application containers do not bind directly to the host’s public network ports; instead, they communicate using service name resolution provided by Docker’s internal DNS.

Docker Network (Bridge Interface)
│
├── nginx (Ingress / Routing Layer)
├── frontend (Next.js Application)
├── backend (NestJS API Engine)
└── database (MySQL Instance)

Container Configuration File (docker-compose.yml)

In the service definitions, the ports section is restricted exclusively to Nginx, allowing other containers to communicate only within app-network.

version: '3.8'

networks:
 app-network:
 driver: bridge

services:
 database:
 image: mysql:8.0
 container_name: database
 environment:
 MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: rootpassword
 MYSQL_DATABASE: app_db
 networks:
 - app-network

 backend:
 build:
 context: ./backend
 dockerfile: Dockerfile
 container_name: backend
 environment:
 DATABASE_HOST: database
 DATABASE_PORT: 3306
 PORT: 4000
 depends_on:
 - database
 networks:
 - app-network

 frontend:
 build:
 context: ./frontend
 dockerfile: Dockerfile
 container_name: frontend
 environment:
 PORT: 3000
 networks:
 - app-network

 nginx:
 image: nginx:alpine
 container_name: nginx
 ports:
 - "80:80"
 volumes:
 - ./nginx/default.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
 depends_on:
 - frontend
 - backend
 networks:
 - app-network

Nginx Reverse Proxy Configuration Details

In Nginx, requests with the /api/ prefix are forwarded to the backend container (backend:4000), and all other root requests (/) are forwarded to the frontend container (frontend:3000).

upstream frontend {
 server frontend:3000;
}

upstream backend {
 server backend:4000;
}

server {
 listen 80;
 server_name localhost;

 location /api/ {
 proxy_pass http://backend/api/;
 proxy_http_version 1.1;
 proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
 proxy_set_header Connection 'upgrade';
 proxy_set_header Host $host;
 proxy_cache_bypass $http_upgrade;
 proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
 proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
 proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
 }

 location / {
 proxy_pass http://frontend;
 proxy_http_version 1.1;
 proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
 proxy_set_header Connection 'upgrade';
 proxy_set_header Host $host;
 proxy_cache_bypass $http_upgrade;
 proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
 proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
 proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
 }
}

Distinguishing Internal States in Port Binding

When architecting container networks, it is critical to accurately distinguish between a container port’s exposed state (Exposed) and its published state to host interfaces (Published).

  • Unpublished Internal State (80/tcp): The socket is LISTENing only on the container’s internal network stack. Direct connections from outside the Docker network (the host OS or external clients) are rejected.
  • Published External State (0.0.0.0:80->80/tcp): Port 80 on all network interfaces of the host OS (0.0.0.0) is forwarded to port 80 inside the container. This enables traffic arriving via public IPs, such as on AWS EC2 or through an ALB, to be correctly forwarded into the infrastructure.

Operational Verification and Status Checks

Following deployment, verify the container run states and the integrity of HTTP responses from the terminal.

$ docker compose ps
NAME IMAGE COMMAND SERVICE CREATED STATUS PORTS
backend app-backend "docker-entrypoint.s…" backend 5 minutes ago Up 5 minutes 4000/tcp
database mysql:8.0 "docker-entrypoint.s…" database 5 minutes ago Up 5 minutes 3306/tcp, 33060/tcp
frontend app-frontend "docker-entrypoint.s…" frontend 5 minutes ago Up 5 minutes 3000/tcp
nginx nginx:alpine "/docker-entrypoint.…" nginx 5 minutes ago Up 5 minutes 0.0.0.0:80->80/tcp, :::80->80/tcp

$ curl -i http://localhost/api/posts
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx/1.25.3
Date: Mon, 17 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 124
Connection: keep-alive
X-Powered-By: Express

Troubleshooting

1. ⚠️ 502 Bad Gateway Error During Nginx Startup

If the application initialization of the upstream backend or frontend containers is not complete when the Nginx container starts, Nginx will fail name resolution or connection establishment and return a 502 Bad Gateway.

  • Cause: While container startup order can be managed via depends_on, the Docker engine alone does not guarantee readiness at the application layer.
  • Resolution: Configure a dynamic resolver in the Nginx upstream block, or integrate health check logic to allow proxy traffic only after dependencies are verified as healthy.

2. ⚠️ Proxy Pass Mismatch Due to Trailing Slash in URI

The presence or absence of a trailing slash in the proxy_pass directive changes the URI path forwarding behavior.

  • proxy_pass http://backend/api/; (with trailing slash): The matched location /api/ portion is replaced, forwarding to http://backend/api/posts.
  • proxy_pass http://backend; (without trailing slash): The original request URI is appended in its entirety.

If a misconfiguration results in a 404 Not Found on the backend, verify consistency between the trailing slash in proxy_pass and the NestJS global prefix configuration.

Configuration Notes

  • 🛠️ Infrastructure Health Verification Criteria: Rather than merely checking that containers are in the Up state, define ALB target group health check endpoints and L7 response codes (HTTP 200 OK) routed through the proxy as monitoring metrics.
  • 🛠️ Least-Privilege Port Publishing Policy: Restrict host port exposure exclusively to Nginx (the proxy tier) and isolate backend and database containers strictly within the internal bridge network to minimize the attack surface.

item.title: Speeding Up Next.js 14 Deployment Pipelines and Resolving Bottlenecks with BuildKit Registry Cache
item.description:
Next.js 14 + Cloud Run Build Optimization: Process of Reducing Build Time from 12 to 4 Minutes

In the pipeline for deploying a Next.js 14 application to Google Cloud Run, a significant bottleneck occurred where the build time exceeded 12 minutes, despite the source code size being only 5.4 MB. This technical log details the optimization methods used to reduce the build time from 12 minutes 7.2 seconds to 4 minutes 23.5 seconds—approximately a 64% reduction—by correcting .dockerignore syntax, removing unnecessary dependencies, implementing Next.js standalone output, and migrating from Kaniko to Docker Buildx with Registry Cache.

1. Analysis of the Factors Behind the 12-Minute Build Bottleneck

The target project is a Next.js application consisting of approximately 60 pages. An audit of the Cloud Build logs, Dockerfile, and cloudbuild.yaml identified the following six factors contributing to the delay:

  1. Invalid .dockerignore: Syntax errors caused large local directories to be included in the build context.
  2. Unused Dependencies: Unnecessary external modules related to Sentry and Module Federation were processed during the build.
  3. Duplicate Build Logic: Type checking via tsc and internal type checking during next build were executed redundantly.
  4. Unoptimized Output Format: Next.js standalone mode was not enabled.
  5. Bloated Runner Stage: Development modules and unnecessary node_modules were included in the final Docker image.
  6. Lack of Layer Cache: Per-build layer caching was not functioning within the ephemeral VM environment of Cloud Build.

2. Basic Optimization (Phase 1)

2.1 Reducing Context by Correcting .dockerignore

In the initial .dockerignore, Markdown escape syntax (e.g., *~, *.md) was incorrectly used, preventing Docker from interpreting them as standard glob patterns. Furthermore, node_modules and .next/cache were not excluded. Consequently, approximately 2.5 GB of node_modules and 909 MB of .next/cache were uploaded as the build context in every cycle. Rewriting the .dockerignore to comply with standard Git syntax reduced the build context size from 3.6 GB to a few megabytes, eliminating the upload overhead.

2.2 Cleaning Up Dependencies and Build Scripts

Unused @sentry/nextjs and @module-federation/nextjs-mf were removed. Sentry, in particular, was generating and uploading global source maps during the build, imposing a heavy load. The SophiProvider component, which dynamically imported obsolete remote modules, was also eliminated. Regarding build scripts, the redundant tsc step was removed since next build performs type checking internally. Static analysis (Lint) was moved to the commit stage to simplify the build pipeline.

2.3 Applying Next.js Standalone and Multi-Stage Builds

By setting output: ‘standalone’ in next.config.js, Next.js traces and outputs only the minimal set of files required for production.

// next.config.js
module.exports = {
 output: 'standalone',
 // ...other configurations
}

The Dockerfile was transitioned to a multi-stage build configuration to copy only the standalone directory and static assets (public and .next/static) into the runner stage. This reduced the final container image size from over 2.5 GB to approximately 400 MB, significantly shortening image push times and Cloud Run cold start durations.

3. Attempted Kaniko Integration and Failure Due to Out of Memory (OOM) (Phase 2)

To utilize layer caching in Cloud Build’s clean VM environment, Kaniko was initially introduced to generate and store cache inside the container image. However, Kaniko loads filesystem snapshots into memory to calculate differences. In an environment with 2.5 GB of node_modules, it exceeded the 8 GB memory limit of the E2_HIGHCPU_8 machine, resulting in an Exit 137 (OOM) error. Although the build eventually succeeded using memory-reduction flags like –compressed-caching=false and –snapshot-mode=redo, the process took 9 minutes 12.8 seconds due to snapshot overhead. This led to the decision to migrate to Docker Buildx.

4. Introducing Docker Buildx and Registry Cache (Phase 3)

The final solution involved adopting the docker-container driver of docker buildx and the type=registry cache, utilizing Artifact Registry as the cache storage. Specifying mode=max ensures all build layers, including intermediate layers, are cached.

# cloudbuild.yaml snippet
steps:
 - name: 'gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker'
 entrypoint: 'bash'
 args:
 - '-c'
 - |
 docker buildx create --use --driver docker-container
 ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)
 docker login -u oauth2accesstoken -p $$ACCESS_TOKEN https://asia-northeast1-docker.pkg.dev
 docker buildx build \
 --cache-from=type=registry,ref=asia-northeast1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/cache/app:latest \
 --cache-to=type=registry,ref=asia-northeast1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/cache/app:latest,mode=max \
 --push \
 -t asia-northeast1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/repo/app:$COMMIT_SHA .

Implementation requires the docker-container driver to explicitly handle credentials, as it does not automatically inherit host credential helpers. A temporary access token is retrieved from the Google Cloud metadata server to perform a docker login inside the container. Bash variables within the Cloud Build YAML must be escaped with double dollar signs ($$ACCESS_TOKEN) to avoid conflicts with substitution parameters.

5. Implementation Results and Performance Verification

The transition of build times across the optimization phases is summarized below:

Build Configuration Total Build Time Status
Initial State (Standard Docker Build) 12 min 7.2 sec Success (No cache)
Kaniko (Initial Attempt) N/A Failure (Exit 137 - OOM)
Kaniko (Memory-reduction flags applied) 9 min 12.8 sec Success
Buildx (First run - Cache generation) 6 min 41.5 sec Success
Buildx (Subsequent runs - Cache hit) 4 min 23.5 sec Success (approx. -64% vs. initial)

The combination of Buildx and registry cache reduced the build time by approximately 8 minutes. Even when packages are modified, only the dependency installation layer is invalidated, preventing the massive delays associated with full filesystem snapshot processing.

Lessons Learned

  • Strict Management of Build Context: Errors in .dockerignore lead to unnecessary gigabyte-scale data transfers, severely degrading CI/CD performance.
  • Selection of Cache Engine: In ephemeral build environments, layer-based registry caching with BuildKit (Buildx) is superior to snapshot-based tools in terms of memory efficiency and execution speed.
  • Future Work: Further speedups will be explored by implementing mechanisms to persist .next/cache between builds and enabling Next.js Incremental Compilation.
